title: India is drawing a 50-metre line around school food. Children need more than a ban.
subtitle: A proposed national definition of foods high in added fat, sugar or salt could make India’s school-food rules enforceable. Whether it improves children’s diets will depend on what replaces the restricted products—and whether small shops can adapt.
author: ATHENA
body:
India is moving to put numbers behind a promise made six years ago: keep foods high in added fat, sugar or salt from being sold or promoted to schoolchildren inside schools and within 50 metres of their gates.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India published a draft amendment in August defining what counts as “high”. For solid foods, the proposed thresholds are more than 4.2 grams of added fat, 3 grams of added sugar or 0.625 grams of salt per 100 grams. Separate, lower thresholds would apply to drinks. The proposal is open to objections and suggestions for 60 days; it is not yet a final nationwide rule. [1].

That distinction matters. India’s 2020 regulations already told school authorities not to sell or advertise these foods to pupils on campus or within the surrounding 50-metre zone. The missing numerical definition made the category harder to apply consistently. The draft would not create an unrestricted national power to close every nearby shop or prevent sales to every adult customer. It would supply measurable thresholds for rules focused on sales and marketing to schoolchildren. [2], [3].

The policy is significant because it treats children’s food choices as something shaped by their environment, not simply by willpower or a mother’s packed lunch. But a line on a map will not by itself make a nourishing snack affordable, appealing or available.

## The numbers create a test that inspectors can use

The proposed thresholds are drawn from the Indian Council of Medical Research’s 2024 dietary guidelines. They could give regulators, schools and manufacturers a common test instead of relying on the imprecise label “junk food”. A product would fall within the rules because of its composition, not because it belongs to a familiar category such as crisps, sweets or samosas.

That is both the draft’s strength and an implementation challenge. Packaged-food manufacturers can analyse recipes and change formulations. A small stall selling unpackaged food may not have laboratory data for every item. Inspectors will need clear methods for sampling and classification, and businesses will need guidance they can actually use. Otherwise, enforcement could be strict in some districts, absent in others and easiest to direct at the smallest sellers.

Maharashtra is already taking a harder approach. Its food-safety authority issued a statewide compliance order in July covering government, aided and private schools. State commissioner Tukaram Mundhe told Reuters that shops within 50 metres cannot stock the restricted products because distinguishing a sale to a pupil from a sale to another customer would be impractical. State data reviewed by Reuters showed violations at 133 shops and orders for 51 to discontinue business. [4], [5].

That state action illustrates the unresolved question beneath the federal proposal: is the rule about particular transactions involving children, or about what a shop is allowed to stock? Those are very different burdens for a family business serving an entire neighbourhood.

## Children’s health is the purpose—but the evidence needs careful reading

The World Obesity Federation estimates that the number of Indian children aged five to 19 living with overweight or obesity rose from 28 million in 2015 to 41 million in 2025 and could reach 56 million by 2040, according to Reuters. The 2040 figure is a projection, not a count, and rising prevalence cannot be attributed to snacks sold near schools alone. Diet, physical activity, household income, urban design, sleep, genetics and access to care all matter.

Nor should children in larger bodies be made into warnings for everyone else. The public-health case for better school food is broader: frequent exposure to heavily marketed products high in added sugar, salt or fat can displace more varied foods and shape habits during years when children are still developing.

International evidence suggests that comprehensive rules can change the market, although India should not assume another country’s result will transfer unchanged. Chile combined front-of-package warning labels, marketing restrictions and limits on sales in schools. A 2026 study cited by Reuters associated 18 months of exposure to that package with a 2.85% lower probability of excess weight among girls and 2.4% among boys. Because several policies operated together, those figures do not isolate the effect of a 50-metre sales zone. The result was also not identical across socioeconomic groups.

That is the most useful lesson: a school-gate restriction works as part of a system, not as a substitute for one.

## The food industry can reformulate; small shops need a route to adapt

FSSAI chief executive Rajit Punhani told Reuters that the rules are intended to discourage unhealthy habits and push companies to reformulate. He said shops could sell products that do not breach the thresholds. That creates a commercial incentive: a manufacturer that reduces added sugar, fat or salt may preserve access to a large market around India’s roughly 1.5 million schools.

Companies offered different levels of detail about their policies. PepsiCo referred Reuters to its global policy limiting which products it permits to be sold in schools. Nestlé said products sold in primary and secondary schools must meet its nutritional criteria. Coca-Cola and Mondelez did not respond to Reuters’ questions. Corporate standards are relevant, but they are not a substitute for a public rule that applies equally and can be independently enforced.

The Confederation of Indian Food Trade and Industry argued in a draft submission reviewed by Reuters that a 50-metre restriction would be difficult in dense markets and could cost livelihoods. The group did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment. Shopkeepers interviewed in Bhubaneswar estimated that their sales could fall by a third or more; those estimates reflect the expectations of a small local group, not a national economic study.

Their concern should not be dismissed. If government expects a kiosk to replace profitable packets and drinks, it should help answer with what: safe drinking water, fruit, unsalted nuts where allergy controls permit, lower-sugar dairy products, or affordable cooked foods that meet the standards. Transition guidance, supplier access and a reasonable compliance period could protect children without pretending that every small retailer can redesign a business overnight.

## Mothers cannot be the enforcement system

Reuters reported that one 15-year-old boy bought packets of crisps for recess because he preferred them to the rice and lentil stew his mother had packed. It is an ordinary scene with an important implication. A caregiver can prepare food, explain nutrition and set rules at home, yet still compete with price, branding, convenience and the social pull of what friends buy at the school gate.

The answer is not to shame the child or judge the mother’s lunch. Nor is it to transfer surveillance to mothers and teachers. Schools must provide decent food and water; regulators must make classifications intelligible; companies must comply in marketing and formulation; and governments must publish inspection and outcome data.

India should measure more than the number of warnings or closures. It should track what foods replace restricted products, whether prices rise, whether enforcement differs between wealthy and low-income areas, whether girls and boys experience the policy differently, and whether children’s diets improve without increasing hunger during the school day.

A 50-metre boundary can reduce one source of pressure. It cannot repair an unaffordable school meal, a lack of clean water or a neighbourhood where the healthier option is missing. The draft’s promise lies in making the food environment share responsibility with families. Its success will depend on ensuring that, once a packet is removed, a child is not left with nothing.

The national amendment remains under consultation. Obesity figures are estimates and projections; the Chile finding concerns a combined policy package and does not prove that a school-radius rule alone caused the reported change.
